episode_title: High-temperature kagome flat bands, proximity transient absorption, and superconductivity's topological floor

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: It's October twentieth, twenty twenty-six, and about sixty new papers hit archive overnight. We're going deep on five of them today: a genuinely two-dimensional kagome lattice with a flat band near the Fermi level, a theory paper predicting fractional Chern insulators in that same material at tens of millielectron-volts, a new flavor of transient absorption spectroscopy that reads out carrier dynamics in one layer through the exciton of a totally different layer, strain disorder from Schottky gates in GaAs two-D electron gases, and a rather elegant theorem about why the 'nicest' Chern bands are actually the worst flat-band superconductors. Let's start with the kagome story.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Right, this is paper one. Kagome materials have been a huge theme for a few years now, but almost always in bulk three-D crystals, where you've got interlayer hopping and multiple orbitals muddying the picture. The pitch here is the first truly two-dimensional kagome lattice.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: They found a van der Waals family, written A-two-T-three-X-four, with alkali metal A, transition metal T is nickel, palladium, or platinum, and chalcogen X is sulfur or selenium. Because the layers are held together by van der Waals bonding rather than ionic or metallic bonding like every other kagome material to date, you can just mechanically exfoliate it down to a monolayer, same as graphene.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the payoff for going 2D is what, exactly? Why not just use the 3D crystal?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Because in 3D the kagome bands hybridize across layers and with other orbitals. Here, the local ligand geometry around each transition-metal site imposes a strong crystal field that isolates a single d-x-y orbital, so you get a clean, textbook kagome band structure: a quasi-flat band sitting right on top of a Dirac crossing, with nothing else nearby in energy.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: How do they actually see this down to one layer? ARPES normally needs a few tens of nanometers of material to avoid charging.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Nano-ARPES, with sub-micron beam spots, and they sandwich the flake between graphene on top and graphite on the bottom. The graphite gives a flat, conductive substrate, the graphene seals it from degradation, and because the kagome material's Brillouin zone is much smaller than graphene's or graphite's, the three sets of bands never overlap in momentum space. They can literally watch the flat band survive, barely dispersing, all the way down to a single layer, with the whole manifold creeping within four hundred twenty milli-electron-volts of the Fermi level due to charge transfer into the graphene.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the headline number is the carrier density.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Because this flat band comes from destructive interference of hopping on an atomic lattice rather than from a moire superlattice, you get roughly one flat-band electron per unit cell instead of per ten-nanometer supercell. That's over two hundred times the areal density you get in twisted bilayer systems. Higher density generally means larger interaction energy scales, so in principle you can push flat-band physics, magnetism, Wigner crystallization, fractional Chern states, up to temperatures way above the sub-kelvin regime moire devices need.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Did they actually dope the flat band, or is this just spectroscopy?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Both. With a bottom graphite gate they shift the flat band by nearly four hundred millivolts in situ under the beam, and in separate dual-gated transport devices they drive an honest insulator-to-metal transition as they push holes into the flat band, three orders of magnitude drop in resistance. Push even further and it goes insulating again, which they can't fully explain with disorder alone and flag as a possible many-body state.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That's the appropriately cautious part. They don't claim to have seen a fractional quantum anomalous Hall state, just that the ingredients, gate-tunable, partially-filled, genuinely two-D flat band, are now all sitting in one real material instead of a moire sandwich.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Which is exactly the setup for paper two, from an overlapping theory group.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: This one takes the DFT-derived band structures from six of these compounds and runs exact diagonalization to map out what correlations actually do to the partially filled flat band. First finding: ferromagnetism is robust over broad filling ranges, and once you're ferromagnetic the active band carries a Chern number, up to three in some of the platinum and selenide compounds.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And from there, fractional Chern insulators?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: A whole cascade. At Jain-sequence fillings they find Laughlin- and Jain-type fractional Chern insulators, an anomalous composite Fermi liquid at half filling that looks like the half-filled lowest Landau level, and competing charge-density-wave phases. The best material, cesium-palladium-sulfur, has the flattest band and the most ideal quantum geometry, and its four-thirds filling fractional state has a many-body gap of about twenty-six millielectron-volts.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: How does that compare to twisted molybdenum ditelluride, where the real fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect was actually measured?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Those gaps are typically one to five millielectron-volts, which is why you need sub-kelvin fridges. Twenty-six meV is roughly five to twenty times bigger, potentially bringing these states into reach of much more pedestrian cooling, and even photoemission.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: What's the catch? This is all exact diagonalization on small finite lattices with a model interaction.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Exactly, they use a phenomenological Ohno interaction tuned to plausible screening, truncate band mixing to at most one virtual excitation, and the system sizes, up to twenty-four or so unit cells, are small enough that some fillings give ambiguous ground states. They're upfront that transport measurements testing for an actual fractional Hall response, and larger-scale methods like DMRG, are the obvious next step. They also throw in a nice follow-up idea: stack two layers with opposite magnetization across an h-B-N spacer and you can get a fractional quantum spin Hall insulator, which is notoriously hard to realize in real materials.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Moving to something squarely in the photoluminescence wheelhouse, paper three, proximity transient absorption.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: The core idea is almost cheeky. In normal transient absorption, you pump a material, then probe an optical transition, and you assume the transient signal reflects carriers living in that same material. These authors ask: what if the probed exciton and the photoexcited carriers are in two different, electronically isolated layers?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Their system is graphene, then a thin h-B-N spacer, then monolayer tungsten disulfide.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Right. They pump at one-point-five-one-two electron-volts, which is well below the tungsten-disulfide gap, so only graphene absorbs. Then they probe near the tungsten-disulfide exciton resonance around two electron-volts. And they see a strong, clearly resonant transient signal at the W-S-two exciton, even through a single layer of h-B-N.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: So the carriers never leave graphene, but they still imprint themselves on a totally different layer's exciton?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Through Coulomb screening across the spacer. The hot carriers in graphene screen the exciton binding in W-S-two, shifting its resonance, and that shows up as differential reflectance. The giveaway is the decay time: the signal decays on about one-point-five picoseconds, graphene's carrier lifetime, not the roughly hundred-picosecond lifetime you'd see from a real W-S-two exciton population.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: How far does this proximity effect reach?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They track it from zero to six layers of h-B-N, roughly two nanometers, and the signal falls off steadily but is still clearly present at six layers. The amplitude also scales linearly with injected carrier density in graphene, giving them a PTA cross section of about one-point-eight times ten-to-the-minus-sixteen square centimeters, only about four times smaller than directly pumping carriers into the W-S-two itself.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: What's this actually good for, beyond being a cute effect?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Two things. One, noncontact optical modulation: you can tune a semiconductor's absorption electrically or optically through a spacer, without ever injecting carriers into the semiconductor, and because graphene's carrier lifetime is sub-picosecond, the modulation bandwidth could reach the hundreds of gigahertz to terahertz range, versus maybe ten gigahertz for direct excitonic modulation. Two, remote sensing, they use the W-S-two exciton as a transducer to read out graphene's own carrier dynamics with about seven times better sensitivity than probing graphene directly. That's attractive for materials that are hard to probe optically on their own, like indirect-gap semiconductors.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Caveats?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: When they remove the h-B-N entirely and put graphene and W-S-two in direct contact, a second resonance appears at a lower energy with a longer decay time, which they attribute to actual hybridized interfacial states rather than pure proximity screening. So the clean proximity picture only holds once you've got that insulating spacer decoupling the layers, without it, you're mixing two different physical mechanisms, and that ambiguity has apparently muddied some earlier graphene-TMD transient absorption papers.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Good cautionary note for anyone doing ultrafast spectroscopy on stacked heterostructures. Now, a step away from optics, paper four, strain disorder from metal gates on GaAs electron gases.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: This is squarely quantum Hall adjacent. Everyone doing fractional quantum Hall transport knows that putting a metal Schottky gate on your two-D electron gas tends to kill the fragile fractional states nearby, and the usual suspect is strain from the mismatch in thermal expansion between the metal and GaAs.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: How do you actually prove it's strain and not, say, charge disorder or pinned impurities in the metal?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They build a clever control: a periodically patterned superlattice gate sitting on top of a uniform thin gate, so the electric potential stays flat everywhere but the strain, which depends on metal thickness, is periodic. At low field this produces commensurability oscillations, Weiss-type oscillations with a period set by the lithographic superlattice spacing, not by the electron density like Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And a uniform, unpatterned gate shows none of that.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Exactly, confirming the oscillations really come from the periodic strain. From the oscillation amplitude they extract a modulation potential of about zero-point-two-nine millielectron-volts, roughly three percent of the Fermi energy, for a hundred-thirty-nanometer-tall array. They also rotate the superlattice relative to the GaAs crystal axes and find the amplitude tracks the known angular dependence of the piezoelectric effect in GaAs, peaking along the crystal's one-one-zero directions, which is about as clean a piezoelectric fingerprint as you could ask for.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Do the COMSOL simulations actually reproduce the numbers, or just the trend?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Both reasonably well, simulated shear strain, piezoelectric potential, and its angular and depth dependence line up with experiment. And it explains the original puzzle: even a boring, unpatterned gate has a granular metal film, and those grain boundaries create their own effectively random strain superlattice that penetrates to the two-D electron gas and scatters electrons, with mobility degrading roughly as thickness to the minus zero-point-eight-five power, consistent with a grain-growth model.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Practical takeaway?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Thinner gates, deeper burial of the electron gas, or an intermediate oxide layer like hafnium oxide all help, though they note burying the two-D electron gas deeper makes it harder to pattern fine features like quantum point contacts, so there's a real design trade-off for anyone building anyon interferometers or similar mesoscopic fractional quantum Hall devices.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Last deep dive, paper five, and this one is more abstract, superconductivity in Chern bands.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Context: fractional Chern insulators are now real, seen in twisted molybdenum ditelluride and rhombohedral multilayer graphene, and some of those same devices also host superconductivity, sometimes in the very Chern band that hosts the fractional states. There's a special class of flat Chern bands called vortexable, meaning you can find a real-space coordinate frame in which the band looks exactly like the lowest Landau level, holomorphic, ideal quantum geometry. Vortexable bands are known to host exact fractional Chern insulator ground states for short-range repulsion.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: So the natural question is whether those same ideal bands are also ideal for superconductivity.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the answer here is no, in fact the opposite. For a band paired with its time-reversed partner through simple on-site attraction, with uniform pairing across the active orbitals, the zero-temperature superfluid stiffness has an exact topological floor set by the Chern number. The authors prove that vortexable bands sit exactly on that floor, they are the least stiff flat-band superconductors you can build at fixed Chern number, filling, and pairing strength. Any enhancement above the floor necessarily costs vortexability.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: What's the mechanism, why would being geometrically ideal make for a worse superconductor?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Both quantities trace back to the same quantum metric, but they're optimized over different spaces. Vortexability is about finding one smooth coordinate map that straightens out the whole band. The superconducting stiffness is set by letting each orbital's Cooper pair relax its phase independently, a much larger space of adjustments. The stiffness-optimal natural embedding is generally not reachable by any single smooth coordinate change, and the gap between the two defines what they call a splitting defect. They verify all this with exact diagonalization and self-consistent Bogoliubov-de Gennes calculations on a few lattice models, including a theta-function-based ideal band and the Qi-Wu-Zhang model, and even work out a physical example in heterostrained twisted bilayer graphene where the defect is nonzero and computable.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: This feels very mean-field and fine-tuned. How much should we trust it for a real material?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Fair concern, the exact results lean on a special solvable class, these so-called quantum-geometric-nesting models with eta-pairing symmetry, and the authors are careful to say they're not claiming the actual superconductivity seen in twisted molybdenum ditelluride is of this type. It's a clean theorem about band geometry and a particular pairing channel, not a prediction for any specific experiment, but it's a sharp, useful constraint for anyone trying to engineer flat-band superconductors alongside fractional Chern physics in the same device.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Good note to end the deep dives on. A few quick briefs before we go. Paper six, Sati and Schreiber, looks at topological quantum gates built from fractional Chern insulators with bounded quantum metric, arguing Chern number above one gives cyclically permuted braiding observables and, in principle, non-Clifford gates like T and CCZ, a theoretical blueprint rather than anything measured.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper seven is a first-principles study of twisted and shifted slabs of the topological insulator bismuth telluride. Naimer and Fabian find that only certain stacking configurations preserve nontrivial topology, creating topological domains at the moire scale, plus pressure-tunable flat bands and unusual radial, rather than tangential, spin-momentum locking in commensurate twisted supercells.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper eight is neutron scattering and DMRG on herbertsmithite, the classic kagome quantum spin liquid candidate. Campello and coauthors find the simulations support two nearly degenerate spin-liquid ground states, one preserving the lattice point-group symmetry and one breaking it, and the measured neutron spectrum is best matched by a mixture of the two rather than either alone.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper nine is a big classification effort, the Anyon Atlas. Berean-Dutcher and colleagues numerically classify topological field theories with up to twenty-two anyon types, using congruence representations of the modular group, and they turn up modular data that can't be built from any known Chern-Simons theory by condensation or gauging, meaning genuinely new anyon theories beyond the usual gauge-theory constructions.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And paper ten, Jin and coauthors run determinant quantum Monte Carlo on the doped Hubbard-Hofstadter model and find that Kohler's rule for magnetoresistance holds surprisingly well across a wide range of interaction strengths and doping, even deep in strange-metal, T-linear-resistivity territory, tied to the onset of local singlet correlations below a crossover temperature of order the hopping scale.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That's the lineup for today.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Kagome flat bands trying to go high-temperature, a transient absorption trick that reads one layer through another's exciton, strain sneaking into every gated two-D electron gas, and a theorem telling the nicest Chern bands they can't have it all. See you tomorrow.

picks.title: Monolayer van der Waals kagome lattice for high-temperature flat-band physics
picks.abstract: Kagome lattice materials host a remarkably rich landscape of novel quantum phenomena, all arising from the intrinsic interplay of topology, correlation, and frustration. While previous studies have been mostly limited to bulk three-dimensional (3D) kagome crystals, the realization of a true two-dimensional (2D) kagome system has remained a long-standing goal, to unlock fundamentally new physics and engineering pathways inaccessible in 3D systems. In this work, we establish the first ideal 2D monolayer kagome lattices by leveraging a novel and versatile van der Waals (vdW) kagome family, A2T3X4 (A = K, Rb, Cs; T = Ni, Pd, Pt; X = S, Se). Our nano-focused angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (nano-ARPES) directly characterizes the electronic structure of A2T3X4 down to the monolayer limit, notably revealing an isolated kagome-derived flat band just below the Fermi level. Via gate-engineering of 2D A2T3X4, the kagome flat band can be further tuned to the Fermi level, allowing direct access to the partially filled flat band physics and establishing a qualitatively new 2D flat band platform. Compared to existing moire-based artificial flat band systems, this vdW kagome-based intrinsic flat band system realizes more than 220 times higher flat band electron density, opening an entirely new density and energy regime for exploring 2D flat band physics. Harnessing this high-electron-density flat band in 2D vdW kagome system provides a clear pathway to scale emergent flat band phenomena - such as fractional quantum anomalous Hall states - to far higher temperatures than currently achievable, as long-envisioned in theory and further supported by our many-body calculations.
picks.why: First realization of an ideal 2D monolayer kagome lattice with nano-ARPES-resolved flat bands at ~220x higher density than moire systems, opening a new high-density flat-band platform directly relevant to 2D material band engineering.

picks.title: Theory of High-Temperature Fractional Chern Phases in Monolayer van der Waals Kagome Materials A2T3X4
picks.abstract: Fractional Chern insulators bring the fractional quantum Hall effect, with its anyonic excitations, to zero magnetic field. So far they have been realized in moiré materials, where the long superlattice period weakens electronic interactions and confines these phases to cryogenic temperatures. Early proposals instead envisioned topological flat bands on atomic-scale lattices, where fractionalization could persist to far higher temperatures, but a suitable material has been lacking. Here we theoretically identify monolayers of the recently synthesized van der Waals kagome family A2T3X4 as such a platform, combining intrinsic topological flat bands and strong Coulomb interactions with gate-tunable carrier density and layer assembly. Exact diagonalization of models derived from density functional theory reveals ferromagnetism over broad filling ranges, supporting diverse fractional Chern insulators, anomalous composite Fermi liquids, and charge-ordered phases. In particular, in Cs2Pd3S4, the fractional Chern insulator exhibits a many-body gap of approximately 26 meV in the largest system accessible with band mixing allowing at most one interband electron-hole excitation. Layer assembly further provides a natural route to fractional quantum spin Hall insulators: bilayers with antiparallel magnetizations support this phase at realistic separations. These results identify an experimentally accessible material family in which chemical composition, carrier density, and stacking offer complementary routes to fractionalization at enhanced energy scales and control over topological order.
picks.why: Companion theory paper predicting fractional Chern insulators, composite Fermi liquids and fractional quantum spin Hall phases at greatly enhanced temperatures in the new vdW kagome family, a major step for FCI physics beyond moire systems.

picks.title: Proximity Transient Absorption in van der Waals Heterostructures
picks.abstract: Transient absorption spectroscopy is a widely used technique for investigating ultrafast electronic dynamics, where transient optical signals are generally interpreted as arising from excitations within the material hosting the probed optical transition. A distinct form of transient absorption spectroscopy, termed proximity transient absorption (PTA), is demonstrated, in which the probed optical transition and the monitored photoexcited carriers reside in different materials. Using graphene/hBN/WS2 heterostructures, photoexcited carriers in graphene induce a strong transient optical response at the excitonic resonance of a WS2 monolayer through Coulomb screening, even when the two layers remain electronically isolated by an atomically thin hBN spacer. The resulting signal follows the carrier dynamics of graphene rather than those of WS2, demonstrating that the WS2 exciton acts as an optical transducer of electronic processes in a neighboring material. The signal decreases systematically with increasing hBN thickness, confirming its proximity origin while remaining substantial for separations approaching 2 nm. PTA provides a noncontact approach for optically modulating one material using photoexcited carriers in another and enables probing of carrier dynamics in materials that are otherwise difficult to investigate directly. More broadly, PTA establishes a new modality of ultrafast spectroscopy and reveals that transient optical signals in van der Waals heterostructures can originate from excitations residing in spatially separated layers.
picks.why: Demonstrates a new 'proximity transient absorption' modality where a WS2 exciton optically reports on photoexcited carrier dynamics in a neighboring graphene layer through an hBN spacer, directly relevant to optical probes of vdW heterostructures.

picks.title: Strain-induced disorder from Schottky gates on high mobility 2DEGs
picks.abstract: Electrostatic gates on two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) in GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures are essential for numerous studies of correlation driven phenomena, many performed within the fractional quantum Hall effect. However, the most commonly used type of gates, the metallic Schottky gate, has the propensity to adversely impact the electron mobility and suppress the fractional quantum Hall states. Here we demonstrate through commensurability oscillations under specially designed nanostructured superlattice gates, that strain effects are responsible for the mobility reduction. The experimental results agree well with COMSOL Multiphysics simulations. In a regular, unpatterned gate the disordered, granular nature of the metal film fills the same role as the superlattice in creating a strain field penetrating down to the 2DEG, as we show with a simplified model. These results will help in understanding, improving and finding novel methods to reduce strain-induced disorder in gated high-mobility 2DEGs.
picks.why: Identifies strain from granular Schottky gate films as the microscopic origin of mobility degradation in high-mobility 2DEGs, a key practical issue for gated fractional quantum Hall experiments.

picks.title: Vortexable Chern Bands Sit Exactly on the Topological Floor of Flat-Band Superfluid Stiffness
picks.abstract: Vortexable Chern bands host ideal fractional Chern insulators. Paired with time-reversed partners by orbital-diagonal on-site attraction, they are the least stiff flat-band superconductors at fixed Chern number C, filling, and pairing amplitude. For uniform pairing and a nondegenerate paired state, the exact T=0 stiffness determinant is the topological floor times 1+(\Torb/2\pi|C|)2\le1+(\TLVP/2\pi|C|)2, where \Torb and \TLVP measure departures from vortexability. Enhancement costs vortexability, and the inequality is strict only if internal components share a site, as in heterostrained bilayers.
picks.why: Derives an exact topological lower bound on superfluid stiffness for vortexable Chern flat bands, sharpening the theoretical foundation for ideal fractional Chern insulators and flat-band superconductivity.

picks.title: Topological Quantum Gates on FCIs with Bounded Quantum Geometry
picks.abstract: Two-band 2D fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) have recently been shown, in principle, to admit unusual anyonic order, associated with Bloch Hopfions localized in momentum space. Here we show that bounding the integrated quantum metric along one primitive Brillouin-zone cycle may refine this topological order to |C| distinct braiding observables, cyclically permuted by lattice translations, for Chern numbers |C| > 1. The cyclic structure entails mildly non-abelian braiding phases and otherwise matches the spectral flow exhibited by the FCI's hybrid Wannier states, with the metric bound equivalently a bound on the states' real-space spread. We give a classification of quantum gates in principle implementable on this topological order; among them we find the non-Clifford T-gate and the non-Clifford entangling CCZ-gate. This points to novel pathways to fault-tolerant quantum processes within the known orbital structure of FCIs, potentially informing experimental searches towards hardware for future topological quantum computers.
picks.why: Shows that bounded quantum geometry in Chern-|C|>1 FCIs can enable non-Clifford topological gates (T-gate, CCZ), a novel link between quantum geometry and fault-tolerant quantum computation.

picks.title: Unconventional spin momentum locking and topological domains in twisted slabs of topological insulator Bi2Te3
picks.abstract: The three-dimensional topological insulator Bi2Te3 hosts topological Dirac states on its two-dimensional surfaces. These Dirac states show spin-momentum locking, which usually implies a tangential Rashba-like spin texture. One can alter the properties of the Dirac states by dividing a slab of such a material into two thinner halves, modifying the interface by twisting, shifting, and changing the interlayer distance. Using first-principles calculations, we investigate such modified slabs of Bi2Te3. The twisting degree of freedom deserves special attention. To this end, we follow two approaches. On the one hand, we probe different stacking configurations in order to extract parameters relevant for small twist angle Moiré structures. We find non-trivial topology only for some stackings, leading to topological domains on the Moiré scale. On the other hand, we calculate the properties of commensurate twisted supercells. The latter reveals not only flat bands, which are tunable by external pressure, but also radial spin textures with unconventional spin-momentum locking.
picks.why: First-principles study of twisted Bi2Te3 slabs reveals moire-scale topological domains and unconventional radial spin textures, extending twistronics concepts to 3D topological insulators.

picks.title: Two quantum spin liquid states coexisting in the kagome antiferromagnet herbertsmithite
picks.abstract: Herbertsmithite (ZnCu3(OH)6Cl2) is one of the most extensively studied quantum spin liquid (QSL) candidates, yet the precise nature of its ground state remains unresolved. Here, we compare the results of high-resolution inelastic neutron scattering on single crystals of herbertsmithite (ZnxCu4-x(OD)6Cl2, x\simeq 0.85) with large-scale density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and dynamical DMRG simulations to benchmark the spin Hamiltonian and uncover fundamental properties of the ground state. The measured spin correlations determine an energy density for the Heisenberg model that closely matches simulations, an essential verification of the Hamiltonian. In parallel, DMRG simulations reveal two nearly degenerate QSL states. Both preserve translational symmetry, but one retains the lattice point-group symmetries whereas the other develops anisotropic spin correlations that break point-group symmetry. These two QSLs have distinct spin structure factors, and, remarkably, close agreement with the neutron spectra is achieved with an admixture of the two states. Our results establish a quantitative correspondence between neutron scattering and simulations, and suggest that herbertsmithite realizes a regime in which two proximate gapped QSL states coexist.
picks.why: High-resolution neutron scattering plus DMRG on herbertsmithite reveals two nearly degenerate, coexisting quantum spin liquid states, resolving a long-standing puzzle in frustrated magnetism.

picks.title: The Anyon Atlas
picks.abstract: We classify possible topological quantum field theories in 2+1 dimensions with up to 22 anyons in the bosonic case and up to 26 in the fermionic case, through the modular data of modular and supermodular tensor categories. We construct such data via congruence representations of SL(2,\mathbbZ) using a numerical optimization algorithm that scales to high rank. We chart the relations between the resulting theories, including anyon condensations and Chern-Simons realizations. We find examples of modular data that do not appear to arise from any Chern-Simons theory by any sequence of condensations of anyons or gaugings of ordinary global symmetries. These examples give qualitatively new topological quantum field theories, which go beyond any notion of gauge theory. For examples in this class with 11 and 12 anyon types, we solve the pentagon and hexagon equations explicitly, showing that these modular data are realized by full unitary topological quantum field theories. We also introduce https://www.AnyonAtlas.org, an online resource for exploring the data.
picks.why: A systematic classification of anyon theories up to 22-26 types uncovers topological orders that cannot be built from any known Chern-Simons theory, a surprising structural result for anyonic/quantum Hall physics.

picks.title: Kohler's Rule Holds in the Strange Metallic Hubbard Model
picks.abstract: Unconventional magnetotransport violating Kohler's rule has been reported in many strongly correlated strange metals, but the exact origin of these violations is yet unknown. To investigate this question, we use determinant quantum Monte Carlo to compute the magnetoresistance of the hole-doped Hubbard-Hofstadter model. Despite T-linear resistivity exceeding the Mott-Ioffe-Regel limit and the nominal absence of well-defined quasiparticles, we find Kohler's rule unexpectedly holds across a wide range of on-site interaction strengths and hole dopings. In particular, Kohler emerges below a crossover temperature T^\star\approx t identified from the double occupancy and specific heat, coinciding with the onset of local singlet correlations between lattice sites. We thus propose that Kohler scaling in this regime reflects a more general form of many-body quantum coherence. Our results show that strong correlations and strange metallicity do not themselves generically produce anomalous magnetoresistance.
picks.why: Large-scale quantum Monte Carlo on the strange-metal Hubbard model finds Kohler's rule unexpectedly holds despite T-linear resistivity and absent quasiparticles, challenging common lore about anomalous magnetotransport.
